questions.prompt: The ultimate-gain experiment, used to tune a PID from one number and one period,
options: raises the proportional gain until the loop oscillates at constant amplitude
applies a step with the loop open and fits a delay
sets the integral gain to zero and the derivative gain to the plant gain
measures the DC sensitivity and stops
questions.explanation: The ultimate gain \(K_u\) is the proportional gain on the stability boundary, and \(T_u\) is the period of that oscillation. A step on the open plant is the reaction-curve experiment, a different test. Zeroing the integral and copying the plant gain is not the procedure. DC sensitivity does not locate the boundary.

questions.prompt: The ultimate-gain PID rule uses \(K_p = 0.6 K_u\). For \(K_u = 5\), the proportional gain is
questions.explanation: \(K_p = 0.6 \cdot 5 = 3\). Using the whole ultimate gain, 5, skips the 0.6 factor and is a more aggressive starting point than the rule. Half of \(K_u\) is 2.5, which is not 0.6.

questions.prompt: The same rule uses \(\tau_i = T_u/2\). For an ultimate period \(T_u = 4\) s, the integral time is
questions.explanation: \(\tau_i = 4/2 = 2\) s. The period itself, 4 s, would be \(\tau_i\) only if the factor were 1. A quarter period, 1 s, is closer to the derivative time than to the integral time.

questions.prompt: Still with \(T_u = 4\) s, the ultimate-gain rule sets \(\tau_d = T_u/8\). The derivative time is
questions.explanation: \(\tau_d = 4/8 = 0.5\) s. Half the period, 2 s, is the integral time from the same rule. The period 4 s is \(T_u\), not \(\tau_d\).

questions.prompt: The reaction-curve method, as opposed to the ultimate-gain experiment,
options: drives the closed loop to the edge of stability
fits a gain, a lag, and a delay to an open-loop step, and never needs the critical gain
works only for plants with no delay
returns the three PID gains with no plant model at all
questions.explanation: A step is applied to the plant alone. The response is summarized by a gain \(K\), a time constant \(\tau\), and a delay \(L\). The ultimate-gain test is the one that sits on the stability boundary. The fit is built for plants that do have a delay. The arithmetic still uses \(K\), \(\tau\), and \(L\).
questions.figure_alt: A delayed rise toward a steady value.

questions.prompt: A plant fit has \(K = 2\), \(\tau = 6\) s, and delay \(L = 1.5\) s. With \(a = KL/\tau\) and the PID rule \(K_p = 1.2/a\), the proportional gain is
questions.explanation: \(a = 2\cdot 1.5/6 = 0.5\), so \(K_p = 1.2/0.5 = 2.4\). Using \(1.2\, a = 0.6\) inverts the rule. The PI coefficient 0.9 in place of 1.2 would give 1.8, which is the next question and not this one.
questions.figure_alt: A delayed rise toward a steady value.

questions.prompt: Lambda tuning of the same first-order-plus-delay plant is usually
options: more oscillatory than the ultimate-gain rule, on purpose
independent of the desired closed-loop time constant
milder, because the designer names a closed-loop time constant \(\lambda\) instead of sitting on the stability boundary
a way to remove the plant delay from the model
questions.explanation: The lambda rule \(K_p = \tau/(K(\lambda+L))\) gets smaller as the requested closed-loop time constant gets larger, so it is the detuned, explicit choice. The ultimate-gain rule does not ask for \(\lambda\). A larger \(\lambda\) is the milder loop. The delay stays in the formula; it is not deleted.
questions.figure_alt: A delayed rise toward a steady value.

questions.prompt: For that same plant, \(a = 0.5\). The PI reaction-curve rule \(K_p = 0.9/a\) gives
questions.explanation: \(K_p = 0.9/0.5 = 1.8\). The PID coefficient 1.2 would give 2.4 on this same \(a\). Using \(0.9\, a = 0.45\) inverts the fraction.
questions.figure_alt: A delayed rise toward a steady value.

questions.prompt: Lambda tuning uses \(K_p = \tau/(K(\lambda+L))\). With \(K = 2\), \(\tau = 6\), \(L = 1.5\), and \(\lambda = 3\), the proportional gain is
questions.explanation: The denominator is \(K(\lambda+L) = 2\cdot 4.5 = 9\), so \(K_p = 6/9 = 0.666667\). Dropping the delay and using \(\tau/(K\lambda) = 6/6 = 1\) is the delay-free rule. The reaction-curve value 2.4 ignores \(\lambda\) entirely.

questions.prompt: Ultimate gain \(K_u = 12\) and ultimate period \(T_u = 1.6\) s. The PID rule gives \(K_p = 0.6 K_u\) and \(\tau_d = T_u/8\). The derivative gain \(K_d = K_p \tau_d\) is
questions.explanation: \(K_p = 0.6\cdot 12 = 7.2\) and \(\tau_d = 1.6/8 = 0.2\), so \(K_d = 7.2\cdot 0.2 = 1.44\). Reporting \(\tau_d = 0.2\) stops one multiplication early. Reporting \(K_p = 7.2\) is the proportional gain, not \(K_d\).

questions.prompt: If the ultimate period is read off a half-cycle and then used as \(T_u\),
options: the derivative time is unchanged, because \(\tau_d\) does not use \(T_u\)
the experiment has to be repeated at a different sample rate before any gain is valid
the integral time \(\tau_i = T_u/2\) comes out half of what the full period would have given
questions.explanation: \(K_p = 0.6 K_u\) does not use the period at all. Both \(\tau_i\) and \(\tau_d\) scale with \(T_u\), so a half-period reading cuts both of them in half. The sample rate is a separate implementation choice and does not repair a misread period.

questions.prompt: A second plant fit has \(K = 4\), \(\tau = 8\) s, and \(L = 0.5\) s. The PID reaction-curve gain \(K_p = 1.2\,\tau/(KL)\) is
questions.explanation: \(KL/\tau = 4\cdot 0.5/8 = 0.25\), so \(K_p = 1.2/0.25 = 4.8\). Using \(\tau/(KL) = 4\) drops the 1.2. Using the previous plant's \(a = 0.5\) gives 2.4 and ignores these new numbers.
questions.figure_alt: A delayed rise toward a steady value.
